perspective:
From Keith’s perspective:

- I am Keith Ndiaye, a construction worker. Elizabeth Sun is my colleague, the receptionist; we have a friendly but professional working relationship.
- Over the past few days, I noticed Elizabeth was unusually curt or short with me. I wondered if I had upset her, possibly through a misunderstanding or a mistake I didn’t know about.
- I asked her if I had done something to upset her. She said no, not at all, and explained she was dealing with personal stuff; she apologized if she seemed short.
- I felt sympathetic. I told her I understood she was going through a tough time, offered to be someone she could talk to, and suggested a coffee break. She said that was kind and accepted.
- During the coffee break, she shared more about her stresses; to me, they seemed severe. I told her I appreciated her sharing and asked if she had considered talking to a professional, saying an external perspective can sometimes help. She said she had thought about it but wasn’t sure and was hesitant about seeking help.
- Afterward, I noticed she became slightly withdrawn. I worried I might have overstepped or embarrassed her, and I felt regretful. I told her I hoped I hadn’t overstepped, and that I only wanted her to know I’m here to support her no matter what. She said I didn’t overstep, appreciated my concern, and said it was just a lot to think about.
- Later, she seemed more open and appreciative of my concern. I believed she valued my support and felt more comfortable around me. I told her I was glad we talked and that I’m always here if she needs to chat or take a break together. She thanked me, said it meant a lot, and that she felt better knowing she had my support.
- I intend to maintain this supportive relationship.

I have no direct access to Elizabeth’s private thoughts or the full details of her personal stress beyond what she told me and how she appeared.
